title: Anagrams: how did LISTEN become SILENT?
description: A small shuffle can turn a cat into an act. Discover the trick behind anagrams, the repeated-letter trap and a few words to try yourself.

cover.alt: Wooden letter tiles arranged as CAT and ACT on a warm tabletop
cover.credit: AI-generated cover image created for BrainiLab.

practice: Try looking at a familiar word from another angle in Connections.

sections.title: The cat has not gained a single letter
sections.html:
Write CAT on three scraps of paper. Slide the C to the middle: ACT. Nothing has been added or thrown away, yet the animal has turned into something you can do.

An anagram rearranges all the letters of a word or phrase to make another word or phrase. The letters move; their counts stay the same. That is the idea in Merriam-Webster’s definition.

LISTEN → SILENT is a pleasing example. It sounds like someone has hidden an instruction inside the word. In fact, the puzzle only needs the matching letters; the meanings do not have to be related.

sections.title: Your letters are a tiny budget
sections.html:
A tempting answer can look right and still spend a letter you do not have. CAT → CATS fails because the S came from nowhere. BOOK → BOO fails because the K has disappeared.

Repeated letters are where this gets sneaky. BOOK gives you two Os, not one. Write the letters in a row and cross off each one as you use it. A valid answer leaves nothing over.

Sorting both words alphabetically is another quick check: LISTEN and SILENT both become EILNST. Their letter budgets match exactly.

sections.title: One stone, two surprises
sections.html:
Take STONE. Can you turn it into something a musician might play? Keep all five letters.

Show one answer

TONES. You can also rearrange STONE into NOTES. Both use S, T, O, N and E exactly once.

If you get stuck, try moving the vowels first. Or look for a familiar ending. Neither trick guarantees an answer, but changing the arrangement can help you stop reading the original word automatically.

sections.title: Same letters, different trick
sections.html:
Anagrams shuffle letters. Palindromes keep the order and read the same backwards. That distinction is handy: CAT and ACT are an anagram pair, but neither word is a palindrome.

For a little challenge, rearrange TEA into a word meaning “consume food”. Then see if there is another real word hiding in the same three letters.

Check your words

EAT fits the clue. ATE uses the same letters too, with the action moved into the past.

questions.prompt: Which word uses every letter of STONE exactly once?
questions.explanation: NOTES rearranges all five letters of STONE. STONES adds an S; TONE and NOSE each leave a letter behind.

questions.prompt: Why is BOO not an anagram of BOOK?
options: Both words must mean the same thing
questions.explanation: An anagram must use all the original letters. BOO leaves the K unused.

questions.prompt: What do LISTEN and SILENT have in common?
options: Exactly the same letters, including the same counts
questions.explanation: Their sorted letters are EILNST. The arrangement and meanings differ, but each letter is used exactly once.
